docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
An example of a client/server [Flutter] / [NestJS]

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude, reviewed by Serge Tahé - September 2026

This document is a translation of the original French version, generated using an automated tool. Some expressions or technical terms may not fully reflect the original meaning.

This course offers a mobile version of RdvMedecins, a doctor’s appointment-booking application: a Flutter client, written in Dart, that relies on a NestJS server exposing a JSON API protected by JWT authentication (ADMIN / USER roles).

It begins with setting up the working environment (Visual Studio Code, Flutter SDK, Android Studio, Android phone and emulator, flutter doctor), then installing the NestJS server, used here as a black box: you run it and test it, without studying its code.

It then introduces Flutter (widgets, StatelessWidget and StatefulWidget, state management with provider), studies the application’s client file by file, and ports the same source code to three families of targets: mobile (Android, iOS), desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux) and web, with the pitfalls specific to mobile.

The course is aimed at readers who already know a web framework (Angular, React or Vue.js) and discover Flutter by comparison: each Flutter concept is related to its equivalent in these frameworks. The basics of the Dart language are presented in the course Introduction to the Dart Language Through Examples.

The same application is built with web clients in the Angular / NestJS, React / NestJS and Vue.js / NestJS courses. To learn Flutter from small examples, see the course Step-by-Step Introduction to the Flutter Mobile Framework.

All courses by Serge Tahé

2.1. Install the tools
docs.text:
1. Node.js: Download and install version 22 (or later) from nodejs.org. Verify the installation in a terminal: 
    node --version
npm --version
  1. Visual Studio Code (VSCode): available for free download at code.visualstudio.com. Install the “TypeScript and JavaScript Language Features” extension (usually already included).
  1. [MySQL] 8: Install, for example, via XAMPP, Laragon (on Windows), or directly via [MySQL] Community Server. A graphical administration tool (phpMyAdmin, [MySQL] Workbench, DBeaver, HeidiSQL…) simplifies the process. Subsequently, the Laragon tool is used.
  2. Postman: available for free download at postman.com.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Android Studio and Android Command-Line Tools
docs.text:
The mobile target for this course is a [Android] phone. To compile the app and install it on this phone, [Flutter] requires the [Android] SDK, which is installed along with [Android Studio], Google’s development environment. [Android Studio] is not used for writing code—the editor remains [VSCode]—it is used here only to install and update the [Android] SDK.

  1. [Android Studio]: Download it for free from [https://developer.android.com/studio] and then install it. When you launch it for the first time, the wizard will offer a standard installation: accept it, and it will download the [Android] SDK.

  1. Open [SDK Manager] from [Android Studio] (the [Tools / SDK Manager] menu when a project is open, or [More Actions / SDK Manager] from the home screen): This is the tool that installs and updates the components of the [Android] SDK.
  2. [SDK Platforms] tab: Verify that a recent [Android] platform is installed (the [Flutter] documentation specifies version 36 at the time of writing).

  1. [SDK Tools] tab: Check [Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)], [Android SDK Build-Tools], and [Android SDK Platform-Tools] (as well as [Android Emulator] if you want to test on an emulator), then click [Apply]. The documentation for [Flutter] also recommends [CMake] and [NDK (Side by side)]. It is the [Android SDK Command-line Tools] packages that are missing when [flutter doctor] displays “cmdline-tools component is missing.”
  2. Accept the licenses for the [Android] SDK by typing the following command in a terminal within the Flutter project, then answering “[y]” to each question until you see the message “All SDK package licenses accepted.”: 
    flutter doctor --android-licenses

[Note]: With version 23.0 of [Android SDK Command-line Tools], the command above may terminate immediately, without prompting for anything, displaying “The --licenses option is no longer needed.” This is a known issue in [Flutter] (issues 191558 and 191487 on github.com/flutter/flutter). Workaround: In [SDK Manager], [SDK Tools] tab, check [Show Package Details], replace version 23.0 of [Android SDK Command-line Tools] with version 22.0, click on [Apply], and then rerun the command.

docs.title: 2.1.3. Create an Android emulator
docs.text:
If you don’t have a phone, you can test the app on a [Android] emulator: a virtual phone that runs in a window on your computer. [Android Studio] installs the [Android Emulator] program (if it was checked in the [SDK Manager], see above) but does not provide a ready-to-use virtual device: you must create one.

  1. [Prerequisite]: Virtualization must be enabled in the computer’s [BIOS], and under [Windows], the [Windows Hypervisor Platform] feature must be checked ([Control Panel / Programs / Turn Windows features on or off]), which requires a restart. Otherwise, the emulator will not start or will remain very slow.
  2. Open [Device Manager] from [Android Studio]: [More Actions / Virtual Device Manager] from the home screen, or [Tools / Device Manager] when a project is open (depending on the version: [View / Tool Windows / Device Manager]).

  1. Click on [Create Device], select a template (for example, [Pixel 8]), then [Next]. Select a recent [Android] system image for the [x86_64] processor and download it using the [Download] link located next to it, then [Next] and [Finish].

  1. Start the emulator using the [Play] button on the [Device Manager], or from a terminal (the first command lists the emulators and their IDs): 
    flutter emulators
flutter emulators --launch <id>

  1. Wait until the [Android] welcome screen appears in the emulator window: the first startup may take several minutes. Then verify that [Flutter] recognizes the emulator, which should appear in the list (for example, [emulator-5554], platform [android-x64]): 
flutter devices

PS C:\Data\st-2026\dev\flutter-nestjs-sept-2026\rdvmedecins_flutter_client> flutter devices
Found 4 connected devices:
  sdk gphone16k x86 64 (mobile) • emulator-5554 • android-x64    • Android 17 (API 37) (emulator)
  Windows (desktop)             • windows       • windows-x64    • Microsoft Windows [version
  10.0.26200.9457]
  Chrome (web)                  • chrome        • web-javascript • Google Chrome 153.0.8010.48
  Edge (web)                    • edge          • web-javascript • Microsoft Edge 153.0.4234.48

[Note]: if [flutter devices] does not display the emulator but instead shows the message “Device emulator-5554 is offline,” the emulator has not finished starting up, or [adb] (the tool that connects the computer to the device, installed along with [Android SDK Platform-Tools]) is in an inconsistent state. Try the following in order: (1) wait for the welcome screen to appear, then rerun the command; (2) restart [adb] using the following three commands (in [Windows], within [PowerShell]), with the last one displaying “device” rather than “offline”; (3) In the [Device Manager], under the device’s [⋮] menu, select [Cold Boot Now], or even [Wipe Data] as a last resort.

& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe" kill-server
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe" start-server
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe" devices

If the problem persists, use [where.exe adb] to verify that no other [adb], of a different version, is present in the [PATH]: Two versions of [adb] competing for the connection cause this issue.

Once the emulator is recognized, the application launches on it with the following command. Note: In the emulator, [localhost] refers to the emulator itself and not the computer; the “Server URL” field must contain [http://10.0.2.2:8080] (see Chapter 5).

flutter run -d emulator-5554

docs.title: 2.1.4. Preparing the Android phone
docs.text:
To run the app on a real [Android] phone, the phone must be set to allow control from the computer:

  1. Enable developer options: open [Settings / About phone], then tap [Build number] several times (usually 7) until the phone indicates that you are a developer. The exact labels vary by manufacturer.
  2. Enable [USB debugging] in the [Developer options] menu (added in the previous step).
  3. Connect the phone to the computer using a USB cable that transfers data (not just charges the phone), and accept the USB debugging permission request on the phone. On Windows, if the phone is not recognized, install the manufacturer’s driver USB (“OEM USB drivers,” see [https://developer.android.com/studio/run/oem-usb]).
  4. Verify that [Flutter] detects the phone: it should appear in the list displayed by the following command, along with the [android] platform: 
    flutter devices

The phone will access the [NestJS] server via the computer’s IP address on the local network (and not via [localhost]): this configuration is described in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 3. Chapter 2 - Installing the [NestJS] server
docs.text:
The [Flutter] client described in this document requires a server to query: the [NestJS] server for the [RdvMedecins] application, included with this document in the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder. Since this document focuses on [Flutter], that server is treated as a “black box”: this chapter explains how to install it, configure it, create its [MySQL] database, launch it, and test it, but does not examine its code. Readers who wish to learn [NestJS] can refer to the document *Introduction to the TypeScript Language and the NestJS Framework* (2026).

This chapter is essentially a reprint of the chapter “Installing a NestJS Server” from the document *Introduction to the Dart Language Through Examples* (2026), adapted for a different server: the tax calculation server in that document is replaced here by the [RdvMedecins] server, and its [dbimpots-2019] database by the [dbrdvmedecins] database.

docs.title: 3.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
To create the [MySQL] database used by the [NestJS] server, we will use the Laragon tool. As of September 2026, Laragon is available at the URL [Download Laragon – Fast & Modern Dev Environment ]. Laragon includes tools that allow you to install a PHP server and the [MySQL] DBMS:

  • in [1], an Apache web server;
  • in [2], the [MySQL] DBMS;
  • in [3], a messaging tool that we will not be using;
  • [4] starts all services (Apache, [MySQL], MailPit);
  • [5] displays the web page for the URL [http://localhost]. By default, this URL refers to the <laragon-install>\www folder, where <laragon-install> is the Laragon installation folder;
  • in [6], launches the HeidiSQL tool, which allows you to manage MySQL databases. We will use this tool to create the database used by the [RdvMedecins] server;
  • In [7], open a terminal where all the binaries needed for Laragon are located in PATH;
  • In [8], open Windows File Explorer to the folder associated with the URL [http://localhost];

The Laragon installation folder contains the following items:

  • In [1], the [bin] folder contains numerous applications:
  • In [1], the Apache web server;
  • in [2], a command-line terminal;
  • in [3], a [git] client for versioning different versions of a project;
  • in [4], a database manager;
  • in [5], a mail manager;
  • in [6], the [MySQL] DBMS;
  • [7], another web server;
  • in [8], [node.js] to run JavaScript scripts;
  • [9], a text editor;
  • [10], the PHP interpreter;
  • [11], the [Python] interpreter;
  • [12], a cache server;

Laragon comes with a comprehensive development environment. In this course, we will use only the [MySQL] DBMS [6] and the [heidisql] tool to manage it graphically;

docs.title: 3.2. Installation and Configuration of the [NestJS] Server
docs.text:
The [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder has the following directory structure:

rdvmedecins-nestjs-server/
├── package.json                  # npm dependencies and scripts
├── tsconfig.json                 # TypeScript compiler configuration
├── nest-cli.json                 # NestJS CLI configuration
├── .env.example                  # template of the .env configuration file
├── database/
│   └── dbrdvmedecins.sql         # database creation script
└── src/
    ├── main.ts                   # server entry point
    ├── app.module.ts             # root module
    ├── config/                   # database connection
    ├── entities/                 # TypeORM entities (one class per table)
    ├── domain/                   # business objects
    ├── repositories/             # data access (DAO layer)
    ├── business/                 # business layer
    ├── web/                      # JSON controller and response models
    └── auth/                     # JWT authentication and roles

Each subfolder of [src/] contains its own [README.md] file, which summarizes the purpose of the files it contains. The source code for these files is not covered in this document.

In the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] folder, type the following commands in a terminal:

npm install
cp .env.example .env

The [.env] file sets environment variables:

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Sample configuration file.
# Copy this file to [.env] then adapt the values to your machine.
# The [.env] file must never be shared or committed (passwords).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

# listening port of the NestJS server (the original Spring server listened on 8080)
PORT=8080

# connection parameters for the MySQL database [dbrdvmedecins]
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=3306
DB_USERNAME=root
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_DATABASE=dbrdvmedecins

# in development only: TypeORM can automatically create/update
# the tables from the entities. It is disabled here because we provide our
# own SQL script [database/dbrdvmedecins.sql], as the original Spring project did.
DB_SYNCHRONIZE=false

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# authentication (see src/auth/)
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# secret key used to sign/verify JWT tokens - MUST be changed
# in production (a long random string, never committed).
JWT_SECRET=change-me-to-a-long-random-string
# validity of a JWT token (see the documentation of the [ms] library:
# "60", "2h", "7d"...)
JWT_EXPIRES_IN=2h

Adapt the newly created [.env] file to your [MySQL] installation (username, password, port). Since authentication was added, this file also contains a key named JWT_SECRET: the example value is suitable for following along with this document, but must be replaced with a random string unique to you before any actual use.

docs.title: 3.3. Creating the Database
docs.text: The [dbrdvmedecins] database mirrors the structure of the original document (2014, Spring 4 / [MySQL] 5): same tables—[doctors], [clients], [slots], [appointments], now with English names—same foreign keys, same uniqueness constraint. The only new addition, introduced by the “authentication” step of this port: the table [users]. The relationships between these tables are as follows: a doctor ([doctors]) has several time slots ([slots], foreign key [doctor_id]); an appointment ([appointments]) links a day, a time slot (and thus a doctor), and a client ([clients]); the table [users] is independent of the other four: it is used solely for authentication.

docs.title: 3.3.1. [database/dbrdvmedecins.sql]
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
  -- Database [dbrdvmedecins] - MySQL 8
  --
  -- This script reproduces EXACTLY the relational schema of the original document
  -- (2014, Spring 4 / Spring Data / MySQL 5): same tables, same columns,
  -- same foreign keys, same uniqueness constraint. Only the database engine
  -- changes its name (MySQL 5 -> MySQL 8), not the structure.
  --
  -- The original document used THREE tables (users, roles,
 -- users_roles) to allow a user to have SEVERAL roles.
 -- Since this application only knows two mutually exclusive roles
 -- (ADMIN, USER), we simplify here to a single [role] column
 -- on the [users] table rather than rebuilding the original many-to-
 -- many relation - a deliberate teaching simplification, documented
 -- in the "Authentication" chapter of the course.
 -- =========================================================================

 -- we start again from an empty database on each run of the script (handy in development)
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS appointments;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS slots;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS doctors;
 DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

 CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
 USE dbrdvmedecins;

 CREATE TABLE doctors (
   id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
   last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
   first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
 );

 CREATE TABLE clients (
   id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   title      VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
   last_name  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
   first_name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
 );

 CREATE TABLE slots (
   id           INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version      INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   doctor_id    INT NOT NULL,
   start_hour   INT NOT NULL,
   start_minute INT NOT NULL,
   end_hour     INT NOT NULL,
   end_minute   INT NOT NULL,
   CONSTRAINT fk_slots_doctor FOREIGN KEY (doctor_id) REFERENCES doctors(id)
 );

 CREATE TABLE appointments (
   id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   day        DATE NOT NULL,
   slot_id    INT NOT NULL,
   client_id  INT NOT NULL,
   CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_slot   FOREIGN KEY (slot_id)   REFERENCES slots(id),
   CONSTRAINT fk_appointments_client FOREIGN KEY (client_id) REFERENCES clients(id),
   CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE (day, slot_id)
 );

 CREATE TABLE users (
   id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
   version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
   login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
   password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
   name     VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
   role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL
 );

 INSERT INTO doctors (title, last_name, first_name) VALUES
   ('Mme', 'PELISSIER', 'Marie'), ('Mr', 'TATOU', 'Paul'), ('Melle','DUPONT', 'Sophie');

 INSERT INTO clients (title, last_name, first_name) VALUES
   ('Mr', 'MARTIN', 'Jean'), ('Mme', 'DURAND', 'Alice'),
   ('Melle','BISTROU', 'Brigitte'), ('Mr', 'GERMAN', 'Luc');

 INSERT INTO slots (doctor_id, start_hour, start_minute, end_hour, end_minute) VALUES
   (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), /* ... */ (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

 INSERT INTO slots (doctor_id, start_hour, start_minute, end_hour, end_minute) VALUES
   (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), /* ... */ (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

 INSERT INTO appointments (day, slot_id, client_id) VALUES (CURDATE(), 2, 3);

 INSERT INTO users (login, password, name, role) VALUES
   ('admin', '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrator', 'ADMIN'),
   ('user',  '$2b$10$6Cvoion7AgJkpYHw5N0jMuWPf8T90J28En56kWBL9PT0bXt7lwW7.', 'User',          'USER');

Let’s comment on this code:

  • Lines 19–23: [DROP TABLE IF EXISTS …] — the script starts with an empty database on each execution, in the reverse order of dependencies (starting with `appointments`, which references `[slots]` and `clients`, all the way down to `users`, which is not referenced by anyone): [MySQL] would refuse to delete a table still referenced by a foreign key;
  • line 47: [doctor_id INT NOT NULL], then line 52: [CONSTRAINT fk_slots_doctor FOREIGN KEY …] — a time slot always belongs to a doctor;
  • line 63: [CONSTRAINT unq1_appointments UNIQUE (day, slot_id)] — the application’s central business rule: the same time slot on the same day can be booked only once. It is this constraint, and this constraint alone, that prevents a duplicate appointment—neither the controller nor the business layer explicitly rechecks it;
  • lines 66–73: [CREATE TABLE users (…)] — the table added by this step. `login` is UNIQUE (two users cannot share the same login ID); `password` stores a password hashed using bcrypt (never in plaintext); role is either 'ADMIN' or 'USER'—a simple text column, whereas the original document used three tables (users, roles, users_roles) to allow multiple roles per user. Since this application requires only two mutually exclusive roles, the original many-to-many relationship would have been more than necessary;
  • lines 90–92: [INSERT INTO users …] — two demo accounts, admin/admin (role ADMIN) and user/user (role USER), with their passwords already hashed using bcrypt (10 rounds of salting)—never in plaintext, including in this demo script.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Running the script with HeidiSQL
docs.text:
To create the [MySQL] database required by the [NestJS] server, we proceed as follows:

  • In [1], all services must be started;
  • in [2], the [Database] option allows you to manage the database;

The [Database] option launches a utility called HeidiSQL:

  • In [1], you can select various DBMS options. The default value provided is MySQL. This is acceptable;
  • in [2], you log in to HeidiSQL;
  • In [1-2], run the SQL file, then select the [dbrdvmedecins.sql] file, which you’ll find in the [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server/database] folder:

Running the [3] file will create the [dbrdvmedecins] database used by the [NestJS] server. To view it, run F5 within HeidiSQL to refresh the display:

The database [dbrdvmedecins] has been created. You can view its contents:

  • In [1-3], the table [clients];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the row’s version number. This number increments each time the row is modified;
    • [title, last_name, first_name] identifies the person;

  • in [1-3], the table [doctors];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the version number of the row;
    • [title, last_name, first_name] identifies the person;

  • In [1-3], the table of doctors’ appointment time slots:
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: row version number;
    • [doctor_id]: foreign key referencing the doctor’s primary key;
    • [start_hour, start_minute]: hour and minutes of the appointment start time. Thus, [8,20] means 8:20 a.m.
    • [end_hour, end_minute]: hour and minutes of the end of the consultation.

  • In [1-3], the [appointments] table of scheduled appointments;
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: version number;
    • [day]: appointment date;
    • [slot_id]: foreign key referencing the primary key of the appointment time slot. Since a time slot is linked to a doctor, we know which doctor is handling this appointment;
    • [client_id]: foreign key to the number (primary key) of the patient attending the appointment;

  • in [1-3], the table [users], which lists the users authorized to use the application [NestJS];
    • [id, version]: primary key, version number;
    • [login, password]: user credentials;
    • [name]: user name;
    • [role]: the user’s role. [ADMIN] has full access rights. [USER] has read-only access. This user can view a doctor’s schedule but cannot schedule or cancel an appointment;

docs.title: 3.4. Starting the [NestJS] server
docs.text:
Start all Laragon services ([Start All]), if you haven’t already. Then start the NestJS server in a VSCode terminal for the NestJS project:

npm run start:dev

The console displays, in order: the startup of the [NestJS] module, the list of routes exposed by the controllers, and then confirmation of startup:

[Nest] RoutesResolver RdvMedecinsController {/}:
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getAllDoctors, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getAllClients, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getAllSlots/:doctorId, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getDoctorAppointmentsOfDay/:doctorId/:day, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getDoctorScheduleOfDay/:doctorId/:day, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getDoctorById/:id, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getClientById/:id, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getSlotById/:id, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/getAppointmentById/:id, GET} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/addAppointment, POST} route
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/deleteAppointment, POST} route
[Nest] RoutesResolver AuthController {/}:
[Nest] RouterExplorer Mapped {/login, POST} route
[Nest] NestApplication Nest application successfully started
[RdvMedecins] NestJS server started on http://localhost:8080

This console output confirms that the server is indeed listening on port 8080—exactly the same port as the Spring Boot server in the original document, which was deliberately chosen for this reason.

These routes constitute the JSON API that the client [Flutter] will consume in Chapter 4. [POST /login] is the only public route: it returns a JWT token that all other routes require in the header [Authorization: Bearer <token>]. The read-only routes ([GET …]) are accessible to the roles ADMIN and USER; the two routes that modify data, [POST /addAppointment] and [POST /deleteAppointment], are reserved for the ADMIN role. Business responses are wrapped in a [{ status, data }] object, where [status] is set to 0 upon success.

docs.title: 3.5. Test the server with a browser
docs.text:
Since authentication was added, all routes in [RdvMedecinsController] require a valid JWT token; therefore, a browser alone can no longer be used to test them directly. For example:

http://localhost:8080/getAllDoctors

now returns a 401 Unauthorized error without a token:

This is the expected behavior: this response confirms that the server is properly protecting its routes. Postman (next section) is required to obtain a token and then use it.

docs.title: 3.6. Testing the [NestJS] server with Postman
docs.text:
The Postman tool is available at URL [https://www.postman.com/downloads/]. You may need to create an account.

Start all Laragon services, then open the Postman desktop application:

  • In [1-2], create a request HTTP to query the doctors’ appointment management server;

docs.title: 3.6.1. Log in and obtain a token
docs.text:
1. Create a new Postman request with the method POST and the URL http://localhost:8080/login;
  2. In the [Body] tab, select "raw," then the JSON format, and enter: {"login": "admin", "password": "admin"} (or "user/user" to test the USER role);
  3. Submit the request.
  • in [1-2], the request POST to the server [NestJS] running on port 8080;
  • to [3-5], the body of the request. This transmits to the server the string JSON containing the credentials of the user attempting to log in, in this case admin/admin;
  • in [6], the server’s response;
  • in [7], the authentication token that subsequent requests must send to the server to indicate “I have already authenticated”;

Copy the value from accessToken: this is the token you must now include in every subsequent request. In the example above, the token to copy is “eyJ...zoM” (without the quotes).

docs.title: 3.6.2. Calling a protected route with the token
docs.text:
For GET /getAllDoctors (or any other route of RdvMedecinsController), in Postman, on the Authorization tab, select the Bearer Token type and paste the token copied above (Postman will then automatically add the Authorization: Bearer <token> header).

  • in [1-2], the request sent to the server. It requests the list of doctors in the database;
  • In [3-5], the request must include the authentication token. In [4], select [Bearer Token], and in [5], paste the authentication token you copied earlier;
  • in [7], the server’s response;

docs.title: 3.6.3. Test the POST routes (/addAppointment, /deleteAppointment)
docs.text:
Follow the same procedure as above (method POST, body JSON, Bearer Token), exactly as the original document used the Chrome extension “Advanced Rest [Client]” for the same routes.

Note: You can find the following Postman requests in the [rdvmedecins-nestJS.postman_collection.json] collection:

In Postman, press Ctrl-0 to load the collection:

  • Click on [1] to load the collection and select the collection file. Once the collection is loaded, it displays its requests:

To test /addAppointment with the token from an account ADMIN:

  1. Postman request, method POST, URL http://localhost:8080/addAppointment;
  2. Authorization tab: Bearer Token, admin token;
  3. [Body] tab, raw, JSON: {"day": "2026-09-13", "clientId": 1, "slotId": 5};
  4. Send the request.

  • in [3-5], the request body;

You can verify with HeidiSQL that an appointment has been added to the database:

To test /deleteAppointment, follow the same procedure with the body {"appointmentId": 2} (the ID of the appointment to be canceled (8) above).

  • in [4], where the number above is the appointment to be deleted;

  • to [5-7], the authentication token;
  • to [9], the server’s response. [status=0] indicates that the operation was successful. You can verify this with HeidiSQL:

  • in [3], appointment #2 no longer exists;

Try this: repeat the same request /addAppointment using the token for the USER account (user/user) instead of the admin token: the response becomes 403 Forbidden, with the message “role [USER] does not allow this action (required role: ADMIN)”—a concrete demonstration of the role-based access control implemented by the server.

docs.title: 3.7. Launch the Flutter client for the first time
docs.text:
In the [rdvmedecins_flutter_client] folder (the [NestJS] server must be started beforehand):

flutter devices          # lists the targets available on this machine
flutter run -d chrome    # web - the simplest target for a first try

The login screen appears first, just as it did for the previous clients in this course (see Chapter 4): two demo accounts are provided with the server database, [admin]/[admin] (role [ADMIN], full access) and [user]/[user] (role [USER], read-only). Two buttons labeled “FR” and “EN” in the upper-right corner allow you to switch the interface to French, even before logging in. Chapter 5 details the equivalent commands for desktop and mobile, as well as the only setting specific to these platforms (the server address; see later in this chapter).

docs.title: 4.1. Sources
docs.text: Official documentation: https://docs.flutter.dev—in particular the pages “What is Flutter?”, “Introduction to widgets,” and “State management.” [Dart] language: https://dart.dev/language

docs.title: 4.2. What Flutter Is Not
docs.text:
This is the most important starting point for this chapter, as it differs significantly from the three previous versions of this course. [Angular], [React], and [Vue.js] all produce [JavaScript]/[TypeScript] COMPILED, which is executed by the [JavaScript] engine already present in a browser—this engine handles all the display work, via [DOM] and [CSS]. A tool like [Cordova]/[Capacitor] (not used in this course) does allow you to package such a web client into a mobile shell, but the client then continues to run in an embedded browser (a [WebView])—never natively.

[Flutter] has nothing to do with any of this. The [Dart] code in this document is compiled, for both mobile and desktop, into NATIVE machine code (compilation [AOT], [Ahead-Of-Time] —the same compilation family as a C++ or Rust program), which is directly executable by the target operating system; it requires NO [JavaScript] interpreter or [WebView] of any kind. [Flutter] includes its own graphics rendering engine ([Impeller], which replaced [Skia] as the default engine on mobile devices): the application draws each of its pixels itself, frame by frame, rather than delegating the display to the operating system’s native widgets (unlike [React Native], which is not used in this course and which instead drives the actual interface components of [Android]/[iOS]). It is this architectural choice that allows [Flutter] to render an identical interface across the three environments targeted by this document - there are no native operating system components whose appearance might vary from one platform to another.

On the [web] target, however, there is obviously no compilation to native machine code: [flutter build web] compiles the [Dart] code to [JavaScript] (or to [WebAssembly], a more recent target), which is executed by the browser—but this generated [JavaScript] does NOT manipulate the [DOM] or [HTML] the way [Vue.js] does: it, too, renders directly onto a single [<canvas>] element (or via automatically generated [HTML] elements, depending on the chosen rendering mode), thereby reproducing the same [Flutter] appearance as on mobile and desktop rather than relying on [HTML] elements styled in [CSS].

docs.title: 4.3. The Flutter development model: everything is a widget
docs.text: [Angular], [React], and [Vue.js]—all three distinguish the LOGIC of a component ([TypeScript]) from its PRESENTATION (a [HTML] template, which may be separate or integrated depending on the framework—see Chapter 4 of the [Vue.js] document for this course, “Components: [.vue] files and [Composition API]”). [Flutter] completely eliminates this distinction: EVERYTHING, within a [Flutter] interface, is a [Widget]—a button, text, margin, alignment, and background color are each a widget, and a complete interface is nothing more than a TREE of widgets nested within one another, described by ordinary [Dart] code (the [build(BuildContext context)] method) rather than by a separate template language—in this respect, [Flutter] takes the choice already made by [React] ([JSX], from [JavaScript], which describes the interface) even further: whereas [JSX] remains a markup language—MIXED with [JavaScript]— [build(...)] simply returns a [Dart] EXPRESSION—nested constructor calls ([Scaffold(appBar: ..., body: Column(children: [...]))])—without any additional syntax to learn.

docs.title: 4.4. StatelessWidget and StatefulWidget: whereas Vue.js requires no distinction
docs.text: [Vue.js] (like [React] and [Angular] before it in this course) makes no structural distinction between a component that has a mutable state and one that does not: [ref(...)] may or may not be called within any [<script setup>], without changing anything in the component’s declaration itself. [Flutter] IMPOSES this distinction right from the class declaration: a [StatelessWidget] (nothing ever changes after its construction—see [ScheduleView] and [LoginPage] in Chapter 4) re-runs its [build(...)] method ONLY when its parameters change; a [StatefulWidget] is paired with a separate [State<T>] class (see [_LoginFormState], [_AppRootState]..., Chapter 4), which holds the mutable state and the method [setState(() { ... })] —the EXPLICIT call that triggers a new rendering, whereas [reactive(...)] on the [Vue.js] side automatically detects every property write. This separation into two classes (Widget/State) is a direct result of a deliberate design choice in [Flutter]: a [Widget] object is IMMUTABLE (rebuilt on every render, like a simple configuration object), whereas its associated [State] SURVIVES from one render to the next.

docs.title: 4.5. Sharing state between widgets: provider, the equivalent of provide/inject
docs.text:
[Vue.js] shares state between remote components via the pair [provide]/[inject]; [React] uses a [Context]; [Angular] uses an injectable singleton service. [Flutter] does not have any of these mechanisms built into the framework itself: the third-party package [provider] (see [pubspec.yaml], Chapter 4), which is virtually indispensable in the [Flutter] ecosystem, serves this purpose. Its principle: a [ChangeNotifier] class (a standard [Dart] class, which can notify its listeners of a change via [notifyListeners()]) is made available to an entire subtree of widgets by a [ChangeNotifierProvider] placed at its root (see [MultiProvider] in [lib/main.dart], which is equivalent to the [app.provide(key, value)] calls on the [Vue.js] side); any descendant widget then re-reads it using [context.watch<MyService>()] (subscribes to future changes—the equivalent of [useXxx()] on the [Vue.js] side) or [context.read<MyService>()] (one-time read, without resubscription—a distinction that [Vue.js] does not need to make).

Key difference from [reactive(...)]: a [ChangeNotifier] does not automatically detect ANYTHING. [reactive(...)] wraps an object in a [JavaScript] proxy that intercepts every property READ and every property WRITE; a [ChangeNotifier] [Dart] is a regular class, and it is up to the developer to explicitly call [notifyListeners()] after every modification that should trigger a new rendering—requiring more manual discipline, in exchange for a mechanism that doesn’t rely on “magic” proxies to understand.

docs.title: 4.6. No separate template language: conditional rendering and lists
docs.text: [v-if]/[v-else] and [v-for] ([Vue.js]) — such as [@if]/[@for] on the [Angular] side, or the ternary operators && and [.map(...)] on the [React] side - are converted, in [Flutter], back into ORDINARY [Dart] expressions, directly within [build(...)]: a classic [Dart] [if]/[else] for a condition, and [.map((element) => Widget(...)).toList()] for a list—the same concept as [.map(...)] on the [React] side, since [Flutter], like [React], does not recognize a separate “template language” distinct from the programming language itself. The [if (condition) ...[ WidgetA, WidgetB ]] syntax (“if collection,” used for example in [lib/app.dart], Chapter 4) takes this logic a step further than [React]: a CONDITION inserted directly within a literal list of widgets, without a ternary operator or intermediate function.

docs.title: 4.7. Dart: a close cousin of TypeScript, not JavaScript
docs.text:
[Dart] was never intended as an alternative to [TypeScript] for the web (unlike the latter, which was specifically designed as a superset of [JavaScript]): it is an independent language, STATICALLY typed from the outset (no implicit “[any]” mode), compiled—never interpreted as-is. For a developer coming from [TypeScript] (like the three previous variants in this course), the essentials translate almost directly: classes, interfaces ([Dart] uses [abstract class] or simple implemented classes, rather than a separate [interface] keyword), generics ([ServerResponse<T>], see Chapter 4), [async]/[await] on [Future<T>] (the EXACT equivalent of [Promise<T>] in [TypeScript]), and a nullability check built into the type system ([String?] rather than a string that is always present—the equivalent of the [strict] mode of [TypeScript], but enforced by the language itself rather than by a compiler option).

A notable difference, encountered in every file in the following chapter that decodes JSON ([core/models/appointment_models.dart]): [TypeScript] removes its types at compile time—a [interface] is checked only at compile time, a decoded JSON object is then used AS IS at runtime ([JSON.parse(...) as ServerResponse<T>], a simple promise made to the compiler). [Dart], on the other hand, has its types determined at runtime: [jsonDecode(...)] always returns dynamic types ([Map<String, dynamic>]), which must be explicitly converted to class instances using a hand-written [fromJson(...)] constructor—more verbose at first, but a missing key or one of an unexpected type then raises an immediate and clear exception, rather than propagating silently.

docs.title: 4.8. A first minimal example
docs.text:
Here is the smallest [Flutter] application that displays something on the screen—compare this with [lib/main.dart]/[lib/app.dart] from Chapter 4, which are significantly more feature-rich but built using the EXACTLY the same building blocks ([runApp(...)], [MaterialApp], and a root widget).

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() {
  runApp(
    const MaterialApp(
      home: Scaffold(
        body: Center(child: Text('Hello, RdvMedecins!')),
      ),
    ),
  );
}

Let's go over this code:

  • Line 1: [import 'package:flutter/material.dart';] — equivalent to [import { ... } from 'vue']: [material.dart] includes all the “Material Design” widgets ([Google]) used in this document—buttons, text fields, app bars, etc. [Flutter] also offers a set of [Cupertino] widgets (with the [iOS] style), which are not used in this course, for those who prefer this style on mobile devices ([Apple]).
  • Line 3: [void main() {] — the entry point of a [Dart] program, EXACTLY like that of a program [C]/[Java] - [Flutter] has no equivalent to the [HTML] of a web page, into which a [main.ts] script would then be embedded: the application launches HERE directly.
  • Line 4: [runApp(...)] — starts the rendering engine [Flutter] and provides it with the root widget to display—the equivalent of [createApp(App).mount('#app')] on the [Vue.js] side ([src/main.ts]), in a single call rather than two.
  • lines 5–9: [MaterialApp(home: Scaffold(body: Center(...)))] — a TREE of nested widgets, each with a specific responsibility: [MaterialApp] configures the theme and navigation; [Scaffold] provides the standard screen structure (area for an application bar, content area, etc.); [Center] centers its child; [Text] displays a string. None of these four widgets is a special case of the language: they are simply [Dart] CLASSES, like the ones this course will write itself in the next chapter.

docs.title: 4.9. Summary: Angular -> React -> Vue.js -> Flutter
docs.text:
See also the [README.md] included with the code for this chapter for the full version.

  • [Angular] components / [.vue] files / [.tsx] files → [Widgets] [Dart] ([StatelessWidget]/[StatefulWidget])
  • [signal()]/[ref()]/[useState()] → mutable fields + [setState(...)] (local state), [ChangeNotifier] (shared state)
  • [input()]/[output()], [defineProps]/[defineEmits], function properties → constructor parameters (inputs), functions passed as parameters (outputs)
  • injectable/composable services + [provide]/[inject]/[Context] → service classes + package [provider]
  • separate template [Angular], [<template>], [Vue.js], [JSX], [React] → method [build(BuildContext)] (pure Dart)
  • [HttpClient]/[fetch] → package [http]
  • [localStorage] → [shared_preferences]
  • No router (single-screen application, in all 5 variants of this course)

docs.title: 5. Chapter 4 - The Flutter client for the RdvMedecins application
5.1. Architecture Overview
docs.text: This client communicates with the course’s [rdvmedecins-nestjs-server] server—which remains strictly unchanged—via the same HTTP routes already documented (POST [/login], GET [/getAllDoctors], GET [/getAllClients], GET [/getDoctorScheduleOfDay/:doctorId/:day], POST [/addAppointment], POST [/deleteAppointment]), with the same JSON envelope [{ status, data }] and the same token-based authentication [JWT] (header [Authorization: Bearer <token>]). For this variant, the overall architecture gains a third component: depending on the chosen compilation target (see Chapter 5), it is no longer just a browser that executes the client, but potentially a mobile or desktop operating system that directly executes the compiled [Dart] code—the server [NestJS], meanwhile, still only processes the same HTTP requests, regardless of the target.

docs.title: 5.2. Project directory structure
docs.text:
rdvmedecins_flutter_client/
├── pubspec.yaml                      project configuration (dependencies, assets)
├── assets/
│   └── i18n/                         translation dictionaries (fr.json, en.json)
└── lib/
    ├── main.dart                     entry point (builds the services, provides them, starts the app)
    ├── app.dart                      root widget (conductor + authentication guard)
    ├── core/
    │   ├── models/                   data classes (mirror of the JSON exchanged with the server)
    │   ├── services/                 SettingsService, AuthService, AppointmentService
    │   ├── http/                     AuthHttpClient (JWT token + logout on 401)
    │   └── i18n/                     TranslationsService (French/English)
    └── features/                     one widget per feature, including the login screen

This directory structure mirrors, folder by folder, that of the [Vue.js] client from this course ([core/models], [core/composables] -> [core/services], [core/interceptors] -> [core/http], [features/] unchanged)—a deliberate choice: the organization of an application is, in most cases, not specific to any particular UI framework.

docs.title: 5.3.1. pubspec.yaml
docs.text:
name: rdvmedecins_flutter_client
description: >
  Flutter client (mobile, desktop and web from one and the same source code)
  for the RdvMedecins application - NestJS / Flutter port of this course.
publish_to: 'none'
version: 1.0.0+1

environment:
  sdk: '>=3.4.0 <4.0.0'
  flutter: '>=3.24.0'

dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter

  # http: the official "low-level" HTTP client of the Dart ecosystem - the
  # strict equivalent of the fetch() used on the Vue.js side (auth.interceptor.ts,
  # appointment.service.ts). Flutter has no fetch() built into the language: this
  # library takes its place.
  http: ^1.2.2

  # provider: the most widespread way of exposing a SHARED state to a whole
  # Flutter widget tree - the exact role played by provide()/inject()
  # on the Vue.js side (settings.composable.ts, auth.composable.ts,
  # language.composable.ts). See the chapter "Introduction to Flutter" for
  # the detailed correspondence.
  provider: ^6.1.2

  # shared_preferences: a persistent key/value storage, available in the
  # SAME way on mobile, desktop AND web - the cross-platform equivalent of
  # localStorage (which, for its part, only exists in a browser).
  shared_preferences: ^2.3.2

  # intl: date formatting (yyyy-MM-dd, see DoctorDayPicker) - the same
  # role as Date.toISOString().slice(0, 10) on the Vue.js/TypeScript side, but
  # explicit rather than a mere string slicing.
  intl: ^0.19.0

dev_dependencies:
  flutter_test:
    sdk: flutter
  flutter_lints: ^4.0.0

flutter:
  uses-material-design: true

  # the translation dictionaries - the equivalent of public/i18n/*.json on the
  # Vue.js side, but EMBEDDED in the application package rather than served
  # by a web server (see Chapter "Porting the application" for the reason
  # for this difference, which precisely concerns the 3 target environments).
  assets:
    - assets/i18n/

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 9–10: [sdk: '>=3.4.0 <4.0.0'] / [flutter: '>=3.24.0'] — equivalent to the [engines] field of a [package.json] [Node.js]: the range of [Dart] and SDK [Flutter] language versions required for this project.
  • Lines 16–20, 22–27, 29–32, 34–37: the four dependencies of this client, each annotated in place with its [Vue.js] equivalent—see also the “Tools Used” section of the introduction.
  • line 42: [flutter_lints: ^4.0.0]—the [Dart] counterpart to [ESLint]: a set of style/quality rules verified by [flutter analyze], which was absent from previous web clients in this course but was automatically generated by [flutter create].
  • Lines 51–52: [assets: - assets/i18n/] — EXPLICITLY declares that all content in [assets/i18n/] must be embedded in the application package; without this declaration, [rootBundle.loadString(...)] (see [core/i18n/translations_service.dart] below) would fail at runtime—a file that exists on disk at the time of [flutter build] is not automatically included in the final package, unlike [public/] in the case of [Vite]/[Vue.js], which is served as-is without prior declaration.

docs.title: 5.4.1. lib/main.dart
docs.text:
Porting [src/main.ts] (client [Vue.js]): builds this client's services, makes them available to the entire widget tree via [provider], and then starts the application.

// =========================================================================
// main.dart
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Entry point of the Flutter client. Equivalent of src/main.ts on the Vue.js
// client side of this course: this file explicitly starts the application
// (runApp(...) here; createApp(...).mount(...) on the Vue.js side) AND
// configures it.
//
// Vue.js configures its application with app.provide(key, value), called
// directly on the application instance - Flutter/provider uses
// a widget, MultiProvider, placed at the root of the tree (see runApp(...)
// below): each ChangeNotifierProvider/Provider it contains makes
// an instance available to the WHOLE subtree it wraps, exactly
// as app.provide(...) did for all descendant components -
// the same idea, expressed as a WIDGET rather than as an imperative
// method call, because EVERYTHING, in Flutter, is a widget (including
// the configuration of a shared state).
//
// The ORDER of the constructions still matters, for the same reasons as
// on the Vue.js side: AuthService(settings) needs settings to already exist
// (to read apiBaseUrl); AppointmentService needs authHttp AND settings.
//
// IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE with Vue.js: createAuthStore(settings) and
// createLanguageStore() on the Vue.js side read localStorage SYNCHRONOUSLY
// during their construction, even before the first render. Their
// Flutter equivalents (AuthService.init(), TranslationsService.init())
// are ASYNCHRONOUS (see their respective files): main() itself must
// therefore become an async function, and WAIT (await) for these two
// initializations BEFORE calling runApp(...) - otherwise the first screen
// displayed would ignore a possibly already stored session or language, for
// the time it takes shared_preferences to answer.
//
// Like the Angular, React and Vue.js clients of this course (a single page,
// no routing table), this Flutter client uses ONLY the minimal
// navigation provided by MaterialApp (essential to showDialog(), see
// features/booking_dialog/booking_dialog.dart): AppRoot (see app.dart)
// displays either the login screen, or the rest of the application, depending on
// AuthService.isLoggedIn - a simple Dart if/else is enough, a routing
// package (go_router or another) would have brought nothing for an application
// with a single screen.
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';

import 'app.dart';
import 'core/http/auth_http_client.dart';
import 'core/i18n/translations_service.dart';
import 'core/services/auth_service.dart';
import 'core/services/appointment_service.dart';
import 'core/services/settings_service.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  // WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized(): essential as soon as one
  // calls a Flutter API BEFORE runApp(...) (here, shared_preferences and
  // rootBundle.loadString(...) in TranslationsService.init()) - without
  // this line, these calls would fail at startup. Vue.js has nothing
  // comparable: the browser is always "ready" even before
  // src/main.ts runs.
  WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();

  // 1. SettingsService first: AuthService and AppointmentService need it
  //    (apiBaseUrl).
  final settings = SettingsService();

  // 2. AuthService: receives settings directly in its constructor, like
  //    createAuthStore(settingsStore) on the Vue.js side - then init() restores a
  //    possibly stored session (see the header comment
  //    above about the asynchronous nature of this step).
  final auth = AuthService(settings);
  await auth.init();

  // 3. the authenticated HTTP layer, then the business service - both
  //    built HERE, only once, rather than inside a widget
  //    (where they would be rebuilt at every render): exactly the same
  //    principle as createSettingsStore()/createAuthStore(...), called only
  //    once before app.mount(...) on the Vue.js side.
  final authHttp = AuthHttpClient(auth);
  final api = AppointmentService(authHttp, settings);

  // 4. TranslationsService: loads the startup dictionary (the
  //    stored language, or the device's language by default) - NO ordering
  //    dependency on the previous steps (unlike
  //    createLanguageStore() on the Vue.js side, which had to wait for
  //    app.use(i18n): this file reimplements everything itself, see
  //    core/i18n/translations_service.dart, so there is no third-party
  //    plugin to install before being able to use it).
  final translations = TranslationsService();
  await translations.init();

  runApp(
    // MultiProvider: groups several providers into a single widget,
    // rather than nesting them by hand (Provider(...) > Provider(...)
    // > Provider(...) > ...) - a readability comparable to the sequence
    // of calls "app.provide(SettingsKey, ...); app.provide(AuthKey, ...);
    // app.provide(LanguageKey, ...);" on the Vue.js side, despite the difference
    // in form (a list of widgets rather than a sequence of statements).
    MultiProvider(
      providers: [
        // .value(...) rather than Provider(create: ...): these instances
        // already exist (built above) - .value(...) simply makes them
        // available to the widget tree, without building
        // new ones. ChangeNotifierProvider, specifically, also subscribes
        // to notifyListeners() and automatically redraws any
        // widget that did context.watch<...>() on this provider (see
        // lib/app.dart) - the role played by the "reactive" nature of a
        // reactive(...) on the Vue.js side.
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: settings),
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: auth),
        ChangeNotifierProvider.value(value: translations),
        // AppointmentService is NOT a ChangeNotifier (nothing, in this service,
        // varies over time once built): a simple Provider
        // is enough, it only makes this instance available, without
        // any notion of notification.
        Provider.value(value: api),
      ],
      child: const RdvMedecinsApp(),
    ),
  );
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • line 60: [WidgetsFlutterBinding.ensureInitialized();] — required whenever you call a [Flutter] API BEFORE [runApp(...)] (here, [shared_preferences] and [rootBundle.loadString(...)])—without this line, these calls would fail at startup; [Vue.js] has nothing of the sort to anticipate, since the browser is always “ready” even before [src/main.ts] is executed.
  • Lines 70–71: [final auth = AuthService(settings); await auth.init();] — MAJOR DIFFERENCE with [createAuthStore(settingsStore)] on the side of [Vue.js], which reads [localStorage] SYNCHRONOUSLY as soon as it is built: [AuthService.init()] is explicitly [async], and [main()] itself must therefore be the same in order to be able to AWAIT before [runApp(...)] — otherwise, the first screen displayed would ignore a session already stored in memory while waiting for [shared_preferences] to respond.
  • Line 89: [await translations.init();] — same note as above regarding the stored language; unlike [createLanguageStore()] relative to [Vue.js], which had to wait for [app.use(i18n)], this step has no sequential dependency on the previous ones: [TranslationsService] reimplements everything on its own, without requiring any third-party plugins to be installed beforehand.
  • Lines 98–116: [MultiProvider(providers: [...], child: const RdvMedecinsApp())] — the equivalent, in the form of a WIDGET rather than imperative calls, of the sequence [app.provide(SettingsKey, ...); app.provide(AuthKey, ...); app.provide(LanguageKey, ...);] on the [Vue.js] side: Each [ChangeNotifierProvider.value(...)] makes a pre-built instance available to the entire subtree.

docs.title: 5.4.2. lib/app.dart
docs.text:
Porting [src/app/App.vue]: the ROOT widget of the application (constructed by [lib/main.dart])—the “conductor” that holds the business state and responds to actions from the [lib/features/] widgets, and the authentication “guard.”

// =========================================================================
// app.dart
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Port of src/app/App.vue (Vue.js client of this course): the ROOT
// widget of the application (built by lib/main.dart). As in the
// three other variants of this course, it is the one playing the role of
// "conductor": it holds the application state (doctors, clients,
// displayed schedule, last doctor/day searched...) and reacts to the actions
// of the "business" widgets of lib/features/ to call the NestJS server at the
// right moment, through AppointmentService.
//
// Since authentication was added, this widget also plays the role of
// "guard": as long as AuthService.isLoggedIn is false, it only displays
// LoginPage (see lib/features/login/); all the server routes being
// protected by JwtAuthGuard, it would anyway be useless (and a source
// of 401 errors) to load doctors/clients/schedule before being logged in.
//
// Two classes, as in the other "stateful" files of this client:
// RdvMedecinsApp (the MaterialApp - the ABSOLUTE root, see lib/main.dart) and
// AppRoot/_AppRootState (the real equivalent of App.vue, with all its state).
// =========================================================================

import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:provider/provider.dart';

import 'core/i18n/translations_service.dart';
import 'core/models/appointment_models.dart';
import 'core/services/auth_service.dart';
import 'core/services/appointment_service.dart';
import 'core/services/settings_service.dart';
import 'features/schedule/schedule_view.dart';
import 'features/booking_dialog/booking_dialog.dart';
import 'features/doctor_day_picker/doctor_day_picker.dart';
import 'features/login/login_page.dart';

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// RdvMedecinsApp: the Flutter root in the strict sense - MaterialApp provides
// the theme, the navigation (Navigator, used by showDialog(), see
// features/booking_dialog/booking_dialog.dart) and the system translations
// (scrolling, dialog boxes...). It is the equivalent, very
// roughly, of what index.html + the app.mount('#app') mounting
// did together on the Vue.js side (src/main.ts) - except that here, this
// "shell" is itself part of the Dart code of the application, rather
// than of a separate HTML file.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class RdvMedecinsApp extends StatelessWidget {
  const RdvMedecinsApp({super.key});

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return MaterialApp(
      debugShowCheckedModeBanner: false,
      // explicit appBarTheme: the default Material 3 theme gives
      // AppBar a light background (colorScheme.surface) - to get back the
      // blue bar with white text of "navbar navbar-dark bg-primary" on the
      // Vue.js side (see App.vue), background and text are set explicitly here,
      // rather than hard-coding a text color on each individual
      // Text() of AppRoot below (see auth.name, further down) - a
      // single source of truth for the look of the bar.
      theme: ThemeData(
        colorSchemeSeed: Colors.blue,
        useMaterial3: true,
        appBarTheme: const AppBarTheme(
          backgroundColor: Colors.blue,
          foregroundColor: Colors.white,
        ),
      ),
      home: const AppRoot(),
    );
  }
}

class AppRoot extends StatefulWidget {
  const AppRoot({super.key});

  @override
  State<AppRoot> createState() => _AppRootState();
}

class _AppRootState extends State<AppRoot> {
  // --- application state -------------------------------------------------
  // the direct equivalent of the ref(...) of App.vue, as simple
  // mutable fields of _AppRootState: setState(...) (see the methods
  // below) stands in for the automatic reactivity of Vue.js.
  List<Doctor> _doctors = [];
  List<Client> _clients = [];
  DoctorDaySchedule? _schedule;
  String? _error;

  // the last search (doctor + day) is remembered to be able to
  // refresh the schedule after a booking or a cancellation - same
  // role as lastDoctorId/lastDay on the Vue.js side.
  int? _lastDoctorId;
  String? _lastDay;

  // reference kept permanently to AuthService, to be able to
  // unsubscribe cleanly in dispose() (see below) - see the
  // comment of initState() below for the reason for this choice.
  late final AuthService _auth;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    // context.read<AuthService>(): when initState() runs, the
    // widget is already properly inserted in the tree (unlike the
    // constructor, where context cannot yet be used for
    // dependency injection) - but context.watch(...) is NOT used
    // here: a StatefulWidget must subscribe to a provider only once,
    // explicitly, never inside initState() with watch()
    // (which assumes a build context). So the reference is kept in
    // a field (_auth) and we subscribe ourselves with addListener(...).
    _auth = context.read<AuthService>();
    _auth.addListener(_onAuthChange);

    // equivalent of "watch(() => auth.isLoggedIn, ..., { immediate: true })"
    // on the Vue.js side: { immediate: true } triggers the callback
    // IMMEDIATELY, without waiting for a first change - useful if a session
    // was already stored (see AuthService.init(), awaited by
    // lib/main.dart before runApp(...)). Vue.js offers this option
    // directly; Flutter has no equivalent mechanism built into
    // addListener(...), so the same effect is reproduced BY HAND: an
    // explicit call right after subscribing, in addition to the subscription
    // itself.
    if (_auth.isLoggedIn) {
      _loadInitialLists();
    }
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    // unsubscribing is ESSENTIAL here: without it, _onAuthChange
    // would keep being called after this widget is destroyed (for
    // example during a hot reload or a route change), and
    // would cause an exception at the first setState(...) on an
    // unmounted widget. Vue.js has nothing comparable to plan for: watch(...) is
    // automatically "cleaned up" when the component that created it is destroyed.
    _auth.removeListener(_onAuthChange);
    super.dispose();
  }

  void _onAuthChange() {
    if (_auth.isLoggedIn) {
      _loadInitialLists();
    }
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // when we become logged in (successful login, or session
  // restored from shared_preferences), the lists of doctors and clients
  // are loaded once and for all.
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  void _loadInitialLists() {
    final api = context.read<AppointmentService>();
    api.getAllDoctors().then((result) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _doctors = result);
    }).catchError((Object err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _error = err.toString());
    });
    api.getAllClients().then((result) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _clients = result);
    }).catchError((Object err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _error = err.toString());
    });
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // reacts to the "Log out" button: clears the session AND the displayed business
  // state - without this, a new user logging in afterwards
  // would briefly see the schedule of the previous one.
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Future<void> _onLogout() async {
    await _auth.logOut();
    setState(() {
      _doctors = [];
      _clients = [];
      _schedule = null;
      _error = null;
      _lastDoctorId = null;
      _lastDay = null;
    });
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // reacts to the call of onSearch(...) by the DoctorDayPicker widget
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  void _onSearchSchedule(int doctorId, String day) {
    setState(() {
      _error = null;
      _lastDoctorId = doctorId;
      _lastDay = day;
    });
    _loadSchedule();
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // reacts to the call of onBook(...) by the ScheduleView widget: HERE, unlike
  // Vue.js (which merely opened the window while
  // remembering slotBeingBooked), the dialog box is opened DIRECTLY
  // with showDialog (through openBookingDialog(...)) and its result is
  // AWAITED - see the header of booking_dialog.dart for the details of
  // this structural difference.
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Future<void> _onBookingRequest(SlotJson slot) async {
    final lastDay = _lastDay;
    if (lastDay == null) {
      return;
    }
    final clientId = await openBookingDialog(context: context, slot: slot, clients: _clients);
    if (clientId == null) {
      return; // the user closed the dialog box without choosing a patient
    }
    try {
      await context.read<AppointmentService>().addAppointment(lastDay, clientId, slot.id);
      _loadSchedule(); // the schedule is refreshed: the slot now appears booked
    } catch (err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _error = err.toString());
    }
  }

  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  // reacts to the call of onCancel(...) by the ScheduleView widget
  // -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Future<void> _onCancelAppointment(AppointmentJson appointment) async {
    try {
      await context.read<AppointmentService>().deleteAppointment(appointment.id);
      _loadSchedule(); // the schedule is refreshed: the slot becomes free again
    } catch (err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _error = err.toString());
    }
  }

  void _loadSchedule() {
    final doctorId = _lastDoctorId;
    final day = _lastDay;
    if (doctorId == null || day == null) {
      return;
    }
    context.read<AppointmentService>().getDoctorScheduleOfDay(doctorId, day).then((result) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _schedule = result);
    }).catchError((Object err) {
      if (mounted) setState(() => _error = err.toString());
    });
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    // context.watch<...>() on the THREE providers the display depends on
    // directly: each call subscribes this widget to the future changes of
    // that provider - if one of them notifies (notifyListeners()), build(...)
    // is called again automatically. This is the mechanism that
    // replaces, here, the automatic reactivity of Vue.js mentioned in
    // core/services/settings_service.dart.
    final t = context.watch<TranslationsService>().t;
    final language = context.watch<TranslationsService>();
    final auth = context.watch<AuthService>();
    final settings = context.watch<SettingsService>();
    // narrow screen (phone in portrait mode): the title bar is lightened
    // (see actions: below), for lack of room to display everything that
    // fits easily on a wide screen.
    final narrow = MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width < 600;

    return Scaffold(
      appBar: AppBar(
        title: Text(t('APP.TITLE')),
        actions: [
          // FR/EN selector: ALWAYS visible (including on the login
          // screen) - the counterpart of the <div class="btn-group"> always
          // displayed in App.vue.
          SegmentedButton<String>(
            segments: const [
              ButtonSegment(value: 'fr', label: Text('FR')),
              ButtonSegment(value: 'en', label: Text('EN')),
            ],
            selected: {language.currentLanguage},
            onSelectionChanged: (choice) => language.changeLanguage(choice.first),
            showSelectedIcon: false,
          ),
          const SizedBox(width: 12),
          // the role badge + name + logout button, for their part, are
          // only displayed once logged in (auth.isLoggedIn) - same
          // condition as the <template v-if="auth.isLoggedIn"> of App.vue.
          if (auth.isLoggedIn) ...[
            Chip(label: Text(auth.role?.asString() ?? '')),
            const SizedBox(width: 8),
            // no hard-coded color style here: this Text() inherits the
            // white foregroundColor set on appBarTheme (see RdvMedecinsApp
            // above), exactly as "navbar-dark" on the Bootstrap side
            // colored all its content in white by default.
            // on a narrow screen, the name is hidden: the role badge and the logout
            // button are enough, and the title bar fits within the width.
            if (!narrow) Text(auth.name ?? ''),
            IconButton(
              tooltip: t('APP.LOGOUT'),
              icon: const Icon(Icons.logout),
              onPressed: _onLogout,
            ),
          ],
          const SizedBox(width: 8),
        ],
      ),
      body: SafeArea(
        child: SingleChildScrollView(
          padding: const EdgeInsets.all(16),
          child: Column(
            crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.start,
            children: [
              // server URL: useful both before and after logging in
              // - extracted into a small dedicated private widget, _ServerUrlField
              // (see below), for the reasons explained next to its
              // definition.
              ConstrainedBox(
                constraints: const BoxConstraints(maxWidth: 320),
                child: _ServerUrlField(settings: settings, label: t('APP.SERVER_URL_LABEL')),
              ),
              const SizedBox(height: 16),

              if (_error != null) ...[
                Container(
                  width: double.infinity,
                  padding: const EdgeInsets.all(12),
                  decoration: BoxDecoration(
                    color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.errorContainer,
                    borderRadius: BorderRadius.circular(4),
                  ),
                  child: Text(
                    _error!,
                    style: TextStyle(color: Theme.of(context).colorScheme.onErrorContainer),
                  ),
                ),
                const SizedBox(height: 16),
              ],

              // not logged in: nothing but the login screen -
              // the exact equivalent of "<Login v-if="!auth.isLoggedIn" />"
              // on the Vue.js side.
              if (!auth.isLoggedIn)
                const LoginPage()
              else ...[
                // widget 1: choice of the doctor and the day
                DoctorDayPicker(doctors: _doctors, onSearch: _onSearchSchedule),
                const SizedBox(height: 16),
                // widget 2: display of the schedule - canEdit hides
                // "Book"/"Cancel" for a USER role
                ScheduleView(
                  schedule: _schedule,
                  canEdit: auth.isAdmin,
                  onBook: _onBookingRequest,
                  onCancel: _onCancelAppointment,
                ),
              ],
            ],
          ),
        ),
      ),
    );
  }
}

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// _ServerUrlField: a small PRIVATE StatefulWidget dedicated to the "Server
// URL" field. On the Vue.js side, this field fits on a single line, directly
// in the <template> of App.vue (<input v-model="settings.apiBaseUrl">):
// v-model itself handles, behind the scenes, the synchronization between the
// displayed field and settings.apiBaseUrl. Flutter has no two-way binding
// built into TextField (see already lib/features/login/login_page.dart): it
// takes a TextEditingController, and therefore an owner able to create it
// and release it (initState/dispose) - an EDITABLE TEXT bound to a
// provider can NOT be a simple StatelessWidget in Flutter, unlike
// an equivalent Vue.js field, which needs no separate
// "component" to exist.
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class _ServerUrlField extends StatefulWidget {
  final SettingsService settings;
  final String label;

  const _ServerUrlField({required this.settings, required this.label});

  @override
  State<_ServerUrlField> createState() => _ServerUrlFieldState();
}

class _ServerUrlFieldState extends State<_ServerUrlField> {
  late final TextEditingController _controller;

  @override
  void initState() {
    super.initState();
    _controller = TextEditingController(text: widget.settings.apiBaseUrl);
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _controller.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return TextField(
      controller: _controller,
      decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: widget.label, isDense: true),
      // onChanged rather than onSubmitted: each keystroke is passed on
      // immediately to SettingsService, exactly as
      // v-model does on the Vue.js side for each typed character (not only on
      // form submission).
      onChanged: widget.settings.setApiBaseUrl,
    );
  }
}

Let’s comment on this code:

  • lines 46–71: [class RdvMedecinsApp extends StatelessWidget] — the root [Flutter] in the strict sense: [MaterialApp] provides the theme and navigation (essential for [showDialog(...)], see [booking_dialog.dart] below) — roughly equivalent to what [index.html] + [app.mount('#app')] did together on the [Vue.js] side.
  • lines 60–66: [appBarTheme: const AppBarTheme(backgroundColor: Colors.blue, foregroundColor: Colors.white)] — replicates the appearance of ["navbar navbar-dark bg-primary"] ([Bootstrap], see [App.vue]): A default [Material 3] theme would give [AppBar] a light background, so it must be explicitly set to restore the familiar blue banner with white text.
  • lines 96–127: [initState()] — reproduces, BY HAND, the equivalent of [watch(() => auth.isLoggedIn, ..., { immediate: true })] on the [Vue.js] side (see [App.vue]): [Flutter] does not have the [immediate] option embedded in [addListener(...)], so you must subscribe THEN explicitly check the current status once—two steps where [Vue.js] requires only one.
  • Lines 129–139: [dispose() { _auth.removeListener(_onAuthChange); }] — INDISPENSABLE: Without this unsubscription, [_onAuthChange] would continue to be called after the widget is destroyed and would cause an exception on the first call to [setState(...)] on a dismantled widget. [Vue.js] has nothing comparable to anticipate, as [watch(...)] is automatically “cleaned up” when the component that created it is destroyed.
  • Lines 203–218: [_onBookingRequest(...)] — HERE is the most visible structural difference in this entire client: rather than opening a “window” by storing a Boolean state (see [slotBeingBooked] on the [Vue.js] side), this widget directly [await]s the result of [openBookingDialog(...)]—see the full comment in [booking_dialog.dart], later in this chapter.
  • Lines 253–256: four [context.watch<...>()] at the beginning of [build(...)]—this widget automatically redraws as soon as any one of these four services (ANY one of them) notifies a change ([notifyListeners()]), exactly the role played by the automatic responsiveness of [Vue.js] for [auth], [settings], and [language] in [App.vue].
  • Lines 260 and 291: [MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width < 600] — the screen (or window) width is used to make the title bar lighter on a phone in portrait mode: the user’s name is hidden ([if (!narrow) Text(...)], a simple [if] Dart in the middle of a list of widgets), while the role badge and the logout button remain visible. On line 276, [showSelectedIcon: false] removes the checkmark that [SegmentedButton] adds to the selected option, which unnecessarily widened the [FR]/[EN] selector. Without these two adjustments, the [actions:] elements of the [AppBar] exceed the width of a phone in portrait orientation.
  • Lines 359–409: [class _ServerUrlField] — a small PRIVATE [StatefulWidget] dedicated to the “server URL” field. As for [Vue.js], this field fit on a single line ([<input v-model="settings.apiBaseUrl">]): [Flutter] does not have a bidirectional link integrated with [TextField], so a [TextEditingController] is required, along with an owner capable of creating or releasing it—an editable text linked to a provider cannot simply be a [StatelessWidget] in [Flutter].

docs.title: 5.5.1. lib/core/models/appointment_models.dart
docs.text:
Port of [core/models/appointment.models.ts], itself copied verbatim from the clients [Angular] and [React]: the classes that describe the format of the JSON data exchanged with the server, with no dependencies on [Flutter]—the “pure” [Dart].

// =========================================================================
// core/models/appointment_models.dart
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Port of core/models/appointment.models.ts (Vue.js client of this course), itself
// copied as is from the Angular and React clients: the Dart classes that
// describe the shape of the JSON data received from the NestJS server. Like their
// TypeScript counterparts, these classes depend on no UI framework
// (no Flutter import here) - this is "pure" Dart, just as
// appointment.models.ts was "pure" TypeScript.
//
// STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE with TypeScript: a TypeScript "interface" is
// a mere description of a SHAPE, checked only at compile time -
// at runtime, a decoded JSON object (JSON.parse) is used AS IS,
// without conversion, and TypeScript "trusts" the developer (see the
// "as ServerResponse<T>" of appointment.service.ts). Dart has no such notion of implicit
// structural typing: jsonDecode(...) always returns dynamic
// types (Map<String, dynamic>, List<dynamic>...), which must be
// explicitly converted into instances of Dart classes through a
// fromJson(...) constructor - present on EACH of the classes below. It is more
// verbose to write once, but the conversion is checked at runtime
// (a missing key or one of the wrong type immediately throws an explicit
// exception), where a wrong TypeScript typing can go unnoticed.
// =========================================================================

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// envelope common to all the server responses (see ServerResponse<T> on the
// NestJS side, and the ServerResponse<T> interface of the Vue.js client).
//
// Dart also generalizes with angle brackets (<T>), exactly like
// TypeScript - the big difference is that here, a mere "as T" is not
// enough to convert the [data] field: the function that knows how to
// build a T from raw JSON must be provided (the [parseData]
// parameter below), because Dart does not know T at runtime
// (type erasure prevents writing "T.fromJson(...)"
// directly).
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class ServerResponse<T> {
  final int status; // 0 = success, anything else = failure (see ResponseStatus on the server side)
  final T? data;

  ServerResponse({required this.status, required this.data});

  factory ServerResponse.fromJson(
    Map<String, dynamic> json,
    T Function(dynamic rawData) parseData,
  ) {
    final rawData = json['data'];
    return ServerResponse<T>(
      status: json['status'] as int,
      data: rawData == null ? null : parseData(rawData),
    );
  }
}

class Doctor {
  final int id;
  final String title;
  final String lastName;
  final String firstName;

  Doctor({required this.id, required this.title, required this.lastName, required this.firstName});
