docs.title: 6. Chapter 5 - Porting the Flutter Application to Mobile, Desktop, and the Web
6.1. A Single Source Code, Multiple Compilation Targets
docs.text:
This is the core of this chapter and the raison d’être of this course variant: NO line of Chapter 4 ([lib/], [pubspec.yaml], [assets/]) changes, regardless of the target selected. “Porting” the application here simply involves choosing a different COMPILATION COMMAND ([flutter run -d <target>] or [flutter build <target>])—never to write, duplicate, or adapt any widgets. This is very different from what a port would have required using the tools covered in the rest of this course: a [Vue.js]/[React]/[Angular] client runs NATIVELY only in a browser—porting it to mobile requires a THIRD-PARTY tool ([Cordova]/[Capacitor], not used in this course) that packages it into a native wrapper containing, in reality, an embedded browser (a [WebView]): the code remains unchanged, but it is STILL NOT a native executable, unlike what [Flutter] produces here for mobile and desktop (see Chapter 3, “What Flutter Is Not”).

The six targets ([Android], [iOS], [macOS], [Windows], [Linux], [web]) are enabled BY DEFAULT in any project created with [flutter create] since [Flutter 3] (see Chapter 1) - No configuration is required on the project side to add one. The only differences from one target to another are: the native compilation tools installed on the development machine ([Xcode], [Visual Studio], [GTK]...), the exact command executed, and—for mobile only—a network configuration detail described later in this chapter.

docs.title: 6.2. Web target
docs.text:
The target already used in Chapter 2 ([flutter run -d chrome]). Two commands are sufficient:

flutter run -d chrome              # development, with hot reload
flutter build web                  # production build, in build/web/

[flutter build web] generates a standalone [build/web/] folder ([index.html], [JavaScript], or [WebAssembly] compiled, resources) - to be deployed on ANY static web server ([Nginx], [Apache], a simple [npx serve]....), exactly like the [dist/] folder generated by [npm run build] on the [Vue.js]/[Vite] side. This build remains a [JavaScript] file served by a browser: it therefore continues to depend on a [NestJS] server REACHABLE from that browser, and thus on [app.enableCors()] (see [src/main.ts] on the server)—which is already active, with no changes required on the server side for this target.

One point to note specific to this target: the “Server URL” field on the login screen (see [_ServerUrlField] in [lib/app.dart], Chapter 4) must then point to an address REACHABLE from the browser running the application—[http://localhost:8080] is acceptable as long as the [NestJS] server is running on the SAME machine as the browser.

docs.title: 6.3. Desktop Target
docs.text:
Three operating systems, three sets of native prerequisite tools (see Chapter 1), but [flutter] commands that are identical in form:

flutter run -d macos               # macOS - requires Xcode
flutter run -d windows              # Windows - requires Visual Studio (C++ Desktop)
flutter run -d linux                # Linux - requires the GTK development packages

flutter build macos                 # production build
flutter build windows
flutter build linux

Each [flutter build <target>] command produces a STANDALONE native executable ([.app] on macOS, [.exe] + its libraries on Windows, a [ELF] binary on Linux), in [build/<target>/]—an executable that, unlike the web build, does not run in ANY browser or on ANY [WebView]: this is native code running directly on the operating system, with its own window and title bar, managed by [Flutter] itself.

This target does not require ANY special network configuration: a desktop application runs on the same machine as the user and accesses [http://localhost:8080] exactly as any other program installed on that machine would (the “Server URL” field on the login screen allows you, as with other targets, to point to a remote server if necessary).

docs.text:
Note: The reviewer has not tested this section.

This is the area that requires the most attention, due to a detail specific to the emulator/simulator network.

flutter emulators                   # lists the configured Android emulators

open -a Simulator                   # starts an iOS simulator (macOS only)

docs.title: 6.5.1. The mobile-specific network pitfall: localhost no longer refers to the development PC
docs.text:
This is THE detail to know for this target, unrelated to [Flutter] itself: [localhost] (or [127.0.0.1]), in the “Server URL” field of the login screen, ALWAYS refers to the machine running the code - and a mobile emulator/simulator is a VIRTUAL machine DISTINCT from the development machine where the server ([NestJS]) is running, even if the two appear to “be on the same computer.”

  • [Android] Emulator (created by [Android Studio]): Use [http://10.0.2.2:8080]—a special address specific to the official [Android] emulator, which automatically redirects to [localhost] on the host machine (the development PC).
  • [iOS] Simulator (macOS only): [http://localhost:8080] works directly, as the [iOS] simulator shares the host machine’s network (unlike the [Android] emulator).
  • Physical device ([Android] or [iOS], connected to the same Wi-Fi network as the development PC): Use the LOCAL [IP] address of this PC on this network (for example, [http://192.168.1.42:8080]), never [localhost] or [10.0.2.2], as both refer to the mobile device itself in this case.

docs.title: 6.5.2. Two additional restrictions specific to the mobile device
docs.text:
• [Android] (since API 28) blocks by default all CLEARTEXT [HTTP] traffic (not encrypted with [https://])—since the server for this course listens on [HTTP] in simple mode, a PRODUCTION-READY [Android] application should declare an explicit exception ([android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"] in the generated [Android] manifest, or a more granular network security configuration)—a native configuration setting, in [android/], outside the [Dart] code presented in this document.
  • [iOS] enforces a comparable policy, [App Transport Security] ([ATS]), which also blocks plaintext [HTTP] by default—an equivalent exception is declared in [ios/Runner/Info.plist] ([NSAppTransportSecurity], [NSAllowsArbitraryLoads], or, more specifically, an exception targeted solely at the development server’s domain).

These two settings apply ONLY to development/demonstration with an unencrypted [HTTP] server, such as the one used in this course—a real production deployment would instead expose the [NestJS] server itself in [https://] (for example, behind a [reverse proxy] as [Nginx]), which would render these two exceptions unnecessary.

docs.title: 6.5.3. A Narrower Screen: The Layout Trap
docs.text:
One final difference specific to mobile devices has nothing to do with the network: a phone in portrait orientation is only about 360 pixels wide (in logical pixels of [Flutter]), compared to several hundred more in a browser or desktop window. A screen designed for a large display can therefore become unusable on a phone: this is what happened to the first version of this document’s client, tested on a [Android] emulator. The doctor/day/button selector ([doctor_day_picker.dart]) aligned three fields within a single [Row], and the title bar ([app.dart]) displayed everything at once: the emulator had to be switched to landscape mode to see everything. Chapter 4 shows the fix. Two rules follow from this:

  • Never assume a width. To choose a layout, check the actual available width—either at a specific location in the tree using [LayoutBuilder] ([constraints.maxWidth]), or for the entire screen with [MediaQuery.sizeOf(context).width]—then choose [Row] (wide screen) or [Column] (narrow screen).
  • Test early on a narrow screen: use the emulator in portrait mode, or a [Chrome] window that you resize to be narrower. In debug mode, [Flutter] indicates that the content is too wide with a yellow and black banner reading “RIGHT OVERFLOWED BY … PIXELS” in the application, as well as a message in the console.

This does not contradict the following observation: the layout adapts based on the screen's SIZE, never the platform—no [if (kIsWeb)] appears. Narrowing a browser or desktop window triggers exactly the same “narrow” layout as a phone does.

docs.title: 6.6. Summary Table
docs.text:
• [web] — [flutter run -d chrome] / [flutter build web] — compiled to [JavaScript]/[WebAssembly], executed by a browser — Server URL: [localhost] (same machine).
  • [desktop] (macOS/Windows/Linux) — [flutter run -d <os>] / [flutter build <os>] — native [AOT] compilation, standalone executable — Server URL: [localhost] (same machine).
  • [mobile] (Android emulator) — [flutter run] — native [AOT] compilation — Server URL: [10.0.2.2] (special address for the emulator).
  • [mobile] (iOS simulator) — [flutter run] — native [AOT] compilation — Server URL: [localhost] (network shared with the host).
  • [mobile] (physical device) — [flutter run] — native [AOT] compilation — Server URL: local [IP] address of the development PC, + exception [cleartext]/[ATS].

docs.title: 6.7. What does NOT change in the Dart code
docs.text: To conclude this chapter, it is worth emphasizing what did NOT need to be written or adapted to cover these three target families: no [if (kIsWeb) { ... } else { ... }] condition appears in Chapter 4, no separate [_mobile.dart]/[_web.dart] file, and no additional abstraction libraries. The few choices already made in Chapter 4 are sufficient, on their own, to make this code portable across the three target families: [shared_preferences] (rather than [localStorage], which is browser-specific) for persistence, [rootBundle.loadString(...)] (rather than a [fetch] to a web server) for embedded translation dictionaries, and the [http] package (rather than a browser-specific API) for networking. This is exactly what the introduction to this document promised: [a single Flutter codebase is enough to build a mobile app, a desktop app and a web app].

docs.title: 7.1. What Has Been Built
docs.text:
This document has adapted the core functionality and authentication of the [RdvMedecins] application from the original 2014 document to current technologies:

  • a complete [NestJS] server (included with this document, installed and tested in Chapter 2, but whose code is not covered here), exposing the same 11 JSON business routes as the original Spring 4 server, on the same port (8080), all of which are now protected by a JWT token;
  • an authentication layer ([@nestjs/passport] + [@nestjs/jwt]): login/password authentication (POST /login), a signed token presented with each subsequent request, and role-based access control ([@Roles]('ADMIN') + [RolesGuard]) on the two routes that modify data;
  • a [Flutter] client (widgets [Material], package [provider]) offering the same features as the original AngularJS 1.x client—selecting a doctor and a date, viewing the calendar, booking and canceling an appointment—supplemented by a login screen, a persistent session ([shared_preferences]), an interface tailored to the logged-in user’s role (booking buttons hidden for the USER role), and the ability to switch the interface between French and English ([TranslationsService], reimplemented without a third-party library).

The core of the database has not changed (same tables [doctors/clients/slots/appointments], same constraints), except for the addition of the table [users]; nor has the general layered architecture—only the tools that implement it have been updated.

Two intentional differences from the original document’s authentication, implemented by the delivered server (see Chapter 2): a JWT token rather than the HTTP Basic header sent with each request, and a single [role] column per user rather than a many-to-many relationship across three tables. A third difference—this one functional—was deliberately chosen for this port: the USER role can now view calendars (read-only), whereas in the original it served only to illustrate a total denial of access.

docs.title: 7.2. What Remains Outside the Scope or to Be Ported
docs.text: Beyond the above, the original document covered three additional topics—one of which has now been addressed, another deliberately left out, and the third deferred to a later stage:

docs.title: 7.2.1. French/English internationalization—addressed in this document
docs.text: The original document proposed switching the interface between French and English using the [angular-translate] library. This port implements this functionality using [TranslationsService] (see Chapter 4), written specifically for this document rather than delegated to a third-party plugin: the fr.json/en.json dictionaries, embedded in the application (and no longer served by a web server), are loaded via [rootBundle.loadString(...)]. Like [angular-translate] and [vue-i18n] before it, [TranslationsService] allows you to switch languages on the fly without reloading the application—a behavior faithful to that of the original document.

docs.title: 7.2.2. The client’s “debug” mode—deliberately excluded from the scope
docs.text: The original document included a technical display mode, activatable from the interface, that provided access to the raw model ($scope AngularJS 1.x) of the current view—a useful feature in 2014, when the development tools available for inspecting an AngularJS application were still limited. This port does not rebuild it: the current [Flutter] development tools ([Flutter] DevTools, usable on all three targets—mobile, desktop, web) now offer, apart from the application itself, a much more comprehensive inspection of the widget tree, their state, and their properties than a custom debugging panel reintegrated into the interface would provide. Adding such a panel would amount to creating a lesser version of a tool already provided by the ecosystem—this decision is therefore final, not merely a postponement.

docs.title: 7.2.3. Artificial network delay—postponed
docs.text: The original document allowed setting an artificial delay before each server response, to observe the interface’s behavior on a slow network (loading indicators, temporary button deactivation, etc.). This feature does not yet have an equivalent in this port.

docs.title: 7.3. A note on the methodology used in this document
docs.text: This document was written by systematically relying on the actual executed code: every server path was tested (including authentication scenarios: successful/failed login, access without a token, access with the wrong role); the [Flutter] client (Chapter 4), on the other hand, was reviewed and verified line by line rather than run by Claude—the environment that produced this document does not have access to a machine capable of running [Flutter] (mobile, desktop, or web), unlike the previous web clients in this course, which can be run directly in an automated [Chromium] browser. The screenshots of the client in Chapters 4 and 5 (web, Windows desktop, Android emulator) were taken by the author on his own machine.

docs.title: 7.4. To take it further right now
docs.text:
While waiting for the next steps in this port, the server and client included with this document provide a ready-to-use foundation for you to experiment on your own:

  • add a new doctor or a new patient (currently, this is done only by modifying the SQL script—a /addDoctor route, also protected by [@Roles]('ADMIN'), could be a first exercise);
  • add a third role, or a user with multiple roles—an opportunity to assess, in very concrete terms, the cost of abandoning the single-column simplification provided by [role] (see Chapter 2);
  • modify the client’s presentation (colors, layout) without changing the server—a good way to verify that the client’s layered architecture works as intended;
  • Review the README file for each folder in the delivered server and client: each explains, in its context, the role of the files it contains.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:

This document is a product of Anthropic’s AI Claude. Its purpose is to adapt the document “An Example of a Client/Server – AngularJS 1.x / Spring 4” in two ways:

  • the AngularJS 1.x client is replaced by a [Flutter] 3 client;
  • the Java Spring MVC web framework is replaced by the web framework [NestJS];

Claude from Anthropic (AI) did most of the work (90%):

  • Code generation: Claude generated all of the code. I simply tested it by following the generated course;
  • Course generation in ODT format: Claude generated several versions at my request. This is where I was primarily involved.

Note 1: If the reader’s primary goal is to “learn NestJS,” an overview of this web framework is available in the document Introduction to the TypeScript Language and the NestJS Web Framework Through Examples. In this document, the NestJS server is treated as a black box. You’ll be shown how to use it, but its code is not described.

Note 2: Flutter’s programming language is Dart. Readers interested in learning the basics of the Dart language can read the course “Introduction to the Dart Language Through Examples” (2026).

Note 3: Claude often refers to the Angular, React, and Vue.js frameworks. Claude has written three courses on these frameworks and remembers them well. That is why he references them:

  • [An Angular/NestJS Client/Server Example (2026)];
  • [A React/NestJS Client/Server Example (2026)];
  • [A Vue.js/NestJS Client/Server Example (2026)];

Note 4: If you feel that Claude’s explanations aren’t sufficient, reach out to Claude to ask for clarification on a specific point in his course. This often helps.

Serge Tahé, September 2026

==

This document is a follow-up to the course “A Client/Server Example - AngularJS 1.x / Spring 4,” written in 2014. That original document built a small application for scheduling medical appointments (“[RdvMedecins]”) using a Spring 4 / Spring Data / Spring MVC server and an AngularJS 1.x client.

Twelve years later, the two frameworks used have evolved significantly—or have even been replaced in common use:

  • on the server side, [NestJS] has established itself as one of the most widely used Node.js/TypeScript frameworks for building structured web applications, with a philosophy similar to that of Spring (modules, controllers, services, dependency injection) but within the JavaScript/TypeScript ecosystem;
  • On the client side, AngularJS 1.x was completely rewritten starting in 2016 under the name [Angular] (versions 2, 4, 5… up to version 22) - The approach taken by the [Angular] / [NestJS] variant in this course: A Client/Server Example—Angular / NestJS (2026). This document takes a different approach: [Flutter] (created by Google, first stable version in December 2018), a “cross-platform” framework: from a single codebase written in the [Dart] language, it generates mobile, desktop, and web applications—whose interface is described not by HTML templates, but by a widget tree (see Chapter 3).

The goal of this document is to revisit the original case study—the same application, the same features, the same database—and to rebuild it using current tools, while maintaining as much of the same instructional progression as the 2014 document as possible.

docs.title: 1.1. A Step-by-Step Reconstruction
docs.text:
The original document was about 300 pages long and covered, in addition to the application’s core functionality—role-based authentication (Spring Security)—twelve progressive examples for learning AngularJS 1.x step by step. Reconstructing all of this content at once would be both time-consuming and difficult to digest.

This document therefore covers the first two steps of the reconstruction:

  • the application’s general architecture (unchanged in principle);
  • the database (unchanged, except for the addition of the [users] table);
  • the installation of the complete [NestJS] server provided with this document, whose appointment viewing and booking/cancellation features are tested using Postman—its code is not covered here, as this document is dedicated to [Flutter];
  • token-based authentication (JWT) and role-based access control (ADMIN/USER) for this server, equivalent to the Spring Security layer in the original document—we will only learn how to use it, first via Postman and then via the client;
  • the corresponding [Flutter] client, with the same features: a login screen, an interface tailored to the logged-in user’s role ([Material Design]), and the ability to switch the interface between French and English ([TranslationsService]).

Two features of the original document are, at this stage, excluded from this document: the original client’s “debug” mode (display of the raw template for the current view), which has been deliberately omitted from this port (see Chapter 6 for the rationale behind this decision), and the configuration of an artificial network delay, which has been deferred to a later stage.

docs.title: 1.2. Who This Document Is Intended For
docs.text:
This document assumes no prior knowledge of either [NestJS] or [Flutter]. Each new concept (decorator, dependency injection, component, signal, etc.) is explained as it appears, in as much detail as possible—even for readers who have never written a single line of TypeScript or Dart.

However, some basic knowledge is helpful for getting the most out of this document:

  • a basic understanding of the Dart language (variables, functions, arrays, objects);
  • a basic understanding of HTTP interactions in a web application (GET/POST methods, JSON format);
  • common tags in the HTML language;
  • using the command line (cd, npm install…).

You do not need to be familiar with the TypeScript language (used on the server side) beforehand: it is a superset of JavaScript that adds a type system, which is explained throughout the document whenever it is used. The same applies to the [Dart] language, used on the client side, which is introduced in Chapter 3. Interested readers may consult the document *Introduction to the Dart Language Through Examples* (2026), which explains Dart in detail.

docs.title: 1.3. The Application Architecture
docs.text:
The overall architecture of the application has not changed since the original document:

  • a web server provides the client with a single interface, built on the Component model (view + associated logic), which relies on services to communicate with the server—a browser for clients [Angular]/[React]/[Vue.js] from this course, or, for this client [Flutter], either a browser, a mobile operating system, or a desktop operating system (see Chapter 5);
  • the user interacts with the views displayed in the browser. Their actions sometimes require a request to the server [NestJS], which processes the request and returns a response JSON (JavaScript Object Notation); this response is used to update the view presented to the user.

The application under consideration will have the following architecture:

  • In [1], the user of the [Flutter] application queries the [Presentation] layer [2] of that application;
  • to perform the action requested by the user, the [Presentation] layer [2] may query the [Services] layer [3];
  • To provide the requested service, the [3] layer may need to query [4], the remote JSON server implemented by [NestJS];
  • Depending on the request received in [5], the [6-8] layers may be queried;
  • the server’s response travels back up layers [2-8] in reverse order;
  • the view displayed to the user, [1], reflects this response;

Note: If you’re confused by the project’s architecture, refer back to this diagram. Note that the DBMS is used by the server, not by the client.

docs.title: 1.4. Tools Used
docs.text:
This document uses the following tools (their installation is detailed in Chapters 1 and 2):

  • Node.js (version 22 or later) and its package manager npm—the equivalent, within the JavaScript ecosystem, of what Java + Maven were for the original Spring server;
  • Visual Studio Code (VSCode), a free code editor, along with its TypeScript extensions—the equivalent of Spring Tool Suite (STS) and WebStorm used in the original document;
  • the [Flutter] SDK (which includes the [Dart] SDK) is installed once, system-wide—unlike [Vite], used by previous web clients in this course, which required no system-wide installation;
  • [MySQL] 8 for the database (the original document used [MySQL] 5—the relational schema itself does not change);
  • [Android Studio] (along with its [Android] SDK and its command-line tools), to compile the application on an [Android] phone, the mobile target for this course—detailed installation instructions are in Chapter 1;
  • Postman (or any other HTTP client), to test the server URLs that respond to POST requests (/addAppointment, /deleteAppointment)—a web browser can only test GET requests.

docs.title: 1.5. Application Features
docs.text:
The “business” features of the [RdvMedecins] application remain unchanged from the original document; access control, however, is slightly more robust than in the original (see the table below):

  • A medical practice employs several doctors, each with their own consultation time slots;
  • a user must log in (username/password) to access the application;
  • Once logged in, the user can select a doctor and a day, and view the doctor’s schedule for that day: each time slot appears either available or booked;
  • a user with the role ADMIN can also book an available time slot for a patient of their choice and cancel an existing appointment;
  • A user with the role USER can view the schedules but cannot book or cancel (read-only access)—a deliberate difference from the original document, where the role USER was used solely to illustrate a denial of access and could not view anything at all (see Chapter 2, section “Creating the Database,” for the rationale behind this choice).

docs.title: 1.7. Organization of this document
docs.text:
1. Setting up the work environment—install the tools and create the [Flutter] project.
  1. Installing the server [NestJS]—install Laragon and the database [MySQL], configure, start, and test the server, then run the client [Flutter] for the first time.
  2. Introduction to [Flutter]—the basics of the framework (widgets, StatelessWidget/StatefulWidget, provider), with a review of concepts already covered in [Angular], [React] and [Vue.js].
  3. The [Flutter] client for the [RdvMedecins] application—the client architecture, each of its files (including the login screen), and a step-by-step walkthrough of the entire application.
  4. Porting the [Flutter] application to mobile, desktop, and web—how a single source code compiles to these three target families, and what you need to know for each of them (network, mobile-specific restrictions).
  5. Conclusion and next steps.
